verdict

/VUR-dikt/ - the stress falls on VUR · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Verdict means the formal decision of a jury or judge in a trial.

Nobody in the village planted an acre until the verdict in the grazing-rights case finally came down.

Example

After the fraud trial, two jurors admitted the verdict had turned on a single exhibit — the second set of account books, kept in the same neat hand but telling a very different story.

Verdict is narrower than 'decision': it is the formal finding a jury or judge returns on the facts — guilty or not, liable or not. Rulings and sentences follow from it, but the verdict itself answers one question: what happened.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

ruling: A ruling is any order a judge issues on a point of law — admit this exhibit, dismiss that motion — and a trial produces rulings all the way through. The verdict is different: the single formal decision on the facts, guilty or not, that the whole case has been building toward.

finding: A finding is one determined fact — the signature was forged, the gate was left open — and a case may pile up dozens of them. The verdict is the final, packaged answer built on those facts: the formal decision on the whole matter, which the court must then act on.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

deadlock: a hung jury — no decision reached at all

mistrial: the case collapses and no verdict ever comes

Where it sits · how much binding force it carries

hunch → opinion → verdict

hunch vs. verdict: A hunch is a private guess with no force at all; hunch stops far short of verdict, the formal finding a court must act on.

opinion vs. verdict: An opinion may be considered and public, but it binds nobody; opinion stops short of verdict, which decides the case.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — ver: true

Root — dict: to say

Put it together: Ver- (true) + dict (to say) = a true saying. Latin verus ('true') meets dicere ('to say'): the verdict is, literally, the truth spoken — the moment the court says what really happened.

Use the root in a new word: predict: Nobody at the observatory would predict anything on the record that year.

Root Check

Word Choice

neutral / legal

In court, verdict is exact — the finding on the facts, nothing more. Outside court it is a light journalistic metaphor ('the verdict on the new bakery: worth the line'), fine in casual prose but worth keeping out of formal legal writing unless a jury really spoke.
